A widely used analgesic and antipyretic for mild to moderate pain and fever. At therapeutic doses it is usually well tolerated; overdose can cause severe liver damage. Do not exceed the maximum daily dose and avoid alcohol.

✅ What it is for: Mild to moderate pain; Fever
💡 How it is taken: It is given orally as tablets, solution or syrup, also as suppositories and, in hospital settings, intravenously.
⚠️ Watch for: Overdose can cause severe liver damage, sometimes with delayed symptoms.

𝗙𝗹𝘂

Flu is a respiratory infection caused by the influenza virus. Unlike the common cold, it begins abruptly with high fever, intense muscle pain, headache and cough. Most healthy people recover within one or two weeks, but it can be severe in older adults, pregnant women and people with chronic diseases. It is prevented by annual vaccination.

Most common symptoms:
• High fever, often 38 °C or more, with abrupt onset
• Intense muscle and joint pain
• Headache
• Cough, often dry
• Sore throat and nasal congestion

A proton pump inhibitor that reduces stomach acid production. Effective for reflux and ulcers. Long-term use is associated with risks such as vitamin B12 or magnesium deficiency and a higher fracture risk; use it under medical supervision.

✅ What it is for: Gastro-oesophageal reflux and oesophagitis; Gastric and duodenal ulcer
💡 How it is taken: It is taken orally, usually once a day, preferably in the morning before breakfast.
⚠️ Watch for: Serious allergic reactions, hypomagnesaemia and vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use, higher risk of digestive infections and fractures.

Taking a medicine correctly is as important as choosing the right one. These general guidelines will help; if in doubt, check the leaflet or ask your pharmacist.

With or without food:
✔️ On an empty stomach: usually before breakfast. The leaflet tells you how long before eating.
✔️ With food: during a meal or just after. This is usually to protect the stomach or help the medicine be absorbed better.
✔️ Take it with a glass of water, unless told otherwise.
✔️ Grapefruit juice, milk and alcohol can change how some medicines work. If you are not sure, ask.

𝗔𝗺𝗼𝘅𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻 · Beta-lactam antibiotics (broad-spectrum penicillins)

An antibiotic from the penicillin family, among the most prescribed in Spain. It treats common bacterial infections of the throat, ears, sinuses, lungs and urine. It does not work for viral infections such as colds or flu, and unnecessary use breeds resistance.

✅ What it is for: Acute streptococcal pharyngotonsillitis; Acute otitis media
💡 How it is taken: Orally, in capsules, tablets or sachets, usually every 8 hours (or every 12 hours in modified-release regimens), with or without food.

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗱

The common cold is a mild viral infection of the upper respiratory tract, very common especially in autumn and winter. It causes nasal congestion, discharge, sneezing, sore throat and cough. It resolves on its own within one or two weeks. It is not treated with antibiotics, which are not effective against viruses. It is managed with rest, hydration and symptom relief.

Most common symptoms:
• Nasal congestion and discharge
• Sneezing
• Sore or itchy throat
• Cough, often dry at first
• Mild headache and general malaise

💡 How it is taken: It is taken orally, twice a day for 5 days (treatment) or once a day (prophylaxis).

✔️ Replace saturated fats (processed meats, pastries, butter) with olive oil, nuts, fish and legumes
✔️ Increase fibre: vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains
✔️ Regular physical activity: at least 150 minutes a week
✔️ Lose weight if overweight and limit alcohol
✔️ Stop smoking

COVID-19 is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. It ranges from mild cases, similar to a cold, to severe pneumonia. The most characteristic symptoms are fever, cough, tiredness and loss of smell or taste. Most people recover at home, but older adults and people with chronic diseases can develop severe illness. Vaccination reduces the risk of severe disease.

Most common symptoms:
• Fever or chills
• Cough, often persistent
• Intense tiredness
• Loss or alteration of smell or taste
• Sore throat and nasal congestion

✅ What it is for: Hypercholesterolaemia; Cardiovascular prevention in at-risk patients
💡 How it is taken: It is taken orally, once a day, at any time of day.
⚠️ Watch for: Rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle breakdown with kidney risk), liver damage and allergic reactions.

𝗕𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘀

Bronchiolitis is a viral infection of the bronchioles, the finest airways of the lung, mainly affecting infants under 2 years. The most frequent cause is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). It causes cough, wheezing and difficulty breathing. Most babies recover at home within one or two weeks, but some require admission. A preventive treatment exists for high-risk infants.

Most common symptoms:
• Nasal congestion and cough
• Wheezing or audible whistling in the chest
• Rapid breathing and respiratory effort (retraction between the ribs)
• Difficulty feeding and reduced milk intake
• Low or moderate fever

✔️ Healthy eating: vegetables, legumes, whole fruit, whole grains and lean protein, reducing ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks
✔️ Regular physical activity: at least 150 minutes a week of moderate exercise, plus strength exercise
✔️ Sustained weight loss if overweight or obese

• Burning or pain when urinating
• Frequent and urgent need to urinate, passing small amounts
• A feeling of not emptying the bladder
• Cloudy urine, strong-smelling or sometimes with visible blood
• Discomfort in the lower abdomen

• Palpitations or a fast heart rate
• Headache, dizziness or tinnitus
